title: Your Brain's 3 AM Night Watch
description:
Documentary case briefing on Why Your Left Hemisphere Stays Awake on Your First Night in a Hotel Bed, grounded in Masako Tamaki (2016) (Current Biology). Empirical findings show that across 35 healthy volunteers, Night 1 in an unfamiliar bed produced significantly shallower slow-wave activity in the left default-mode network than in the right hemisphere.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how prefrontal cortex, thalamus, amygdala coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that the bigger the inter-hemispheric slow-wave asymmetry between left and right hemispheres, the longer volunteers took to fall asleep on Night 1.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Masako Tamaki, Ji Won Bang, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki (2016). Night Watch in One Brain Hemisphere during Sleep Associated with the First-Night Effect in Humans. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2016.02.063
- H. W. Agnew, Wilse B. Webb, Robert L. Williams (1966). THE FIRST NIGHT EFFECT: AN EEG STUDYOF SLEEP. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8986.1966.tb02650.x
- Alejandro Osorio-Forero, Georgios Foustoukos, Romain Cardis, Najma Cherrad, Christiane Devenoges, Laura M. J. Fernandez, Anita Lüthi (2025). Infraslow noradrenergic locus coeruleus activity fluctuations are gatekeepers of the NREM–REM sleep cycle. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-024-01822-0

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
